questions.question: What is the defining curve equation for secp256k1 over its prime field?
options: y² ≡ x³ + 7 (mod p)
y² ≡ x³ + x + 7 (mod p)
y² ≡ x³ + 486662·x² + x (mod p)
y² ≡ x³ + ax² + b (mod 2)
questions.explanation: secp256k1 is the short-Weierstrass curve y² = x³ + 7 over a prime field.

questions.question: What does a compressed secp256k1 public key typically contain?
options: A 1-byte prefix (02/03) and a 32-byte x-coordinate
A 1-byte prefix (04) and 32-byte x and y coordinates
A 32-byte x-coordinate and a 32-byte y-coordinate (no prefix)
A 32-byte scalar and a 32-byte u-coordinate
questions.explanation: Compressed SEC1-style encodings keep x and one bit of information via the 02/03 prefix.

questions.question: In a compressed secp256k1 public key, what information does the first byte (0x02 or 0x03) encode?
options: Whether the y-coordinate is even or odd
Whether the x-coordinate is even or odd
Whether the point is in the correct subgroup
Whether the scalar was reduced modulo n
questions.explanation: The prefix selects which of the two possible y values (y or −y mod p) to use by encoding y parity.

questions.question: Why is it possible to reconstruct the full point (x, y) from a compressed key that only includes x plus one bit?
options: For a given x, the curve equation yields 0 or 2 y values, and they differ by sign (y and −y)
For a given x, the curve equation yields exactly one y value for every x in the field
The missing y-coordinate is always 0 for secp256k1 points
The missing y-coordinate is recovered by hashing x with SHA-256
questions.explanation: Over a prime field, solutions for y come in pairs (y, −y) when they exist, so one extra bit disambiguates.

questions.question: For secp256k1, p ≡ 3 (mod 4). What does this enable for computing square roots modulo p (when they exist)?
options: Compute sqrt(a) as a^((p+1)/4) (mod p) and verify the result
Compute sqrt(a) as a^(p−1) (mod p) without any verification
Compute sqrt(a) as a^((p−1)/2) (mod p) and use it directly as the root
Avoid modular square roots entirely because secp256k1 uses only x-coordinates
questions.explanation: When p ≡ 3 (mod 4), exponentiation to (p+1)/4 yields a square root for quadratic residues, and you still verify x² ≡ a.

questions.question: Attack scenario: what information can leak from a naive double-and-add scalar multiplication implementation?
options: Scalar bits can leak because additions occur only when a bit is 1
The field prime p can be recovered from a single public key
The discrete logarithm problem becomes easy because the curve has a = 0
Public keys can be forged because compressed keys omit y
questions.explanation: If an attacker can distinguish “double only” from “double+add” (timing/power/cache), they learn information about secret bits.

questions.question: What is the standard validity range for a secp256k1 private key scalar k, assuming the group order is n?
options: 1 ≤ k < n
0 ≤ k ≤ n
1 ≤ k ≤ p
0 ≤ k < p
questions.explanation: Private scalars are taken modulo n, but 0 is rejected; the conventional range is 1..n−1.

questions.question: When parsing an uncompressed secp256k1 public key (04 || x || y), which check is essential to prevent accepting invalid points?
options: Verify that (x, y) satisfies y² ≡ x³ + 7 (mod p)
Verify that x is less than n (the group order)
Verify that the byte string is little-endian encoded
Verify that x has an even least significant bit
questions.explanation: The core validity check is “on-curve”: the coordinates must satisfy the curve equation modulo p.
